## 3. Q1: TMA + wgmma skinny GEMM for m in {16, 32, 128, 256}

### 3.1 Shape of the kernel

Swap-AB: `D[64 rows of W, N = tokens] = W_tile[64, K] * x^T[K, N]`. W is the wgmma A operand
from shared memory (64 x 16 per instruction, K-major, which is W's natural row-major layout),
x^T is the B operand from shared memory (N x 16 per instruction, K-major, which is x's
natural layout). No transposes, no repack of x. Both operands are BF16 with FP32 accumulation
(`wgmma.mma_async.sync.aligned.m64nNk16.f32.bf16.bf16`). The output tile is [rows, tokens], the
transpose of `out[t, n]`, so the epilogue goes through shared memory once (section 3.6).

Token padding: N must be a multiple of 8 and at most 256. Instantiate N in
{8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256} only (all of these exist as CUTLASS atoms, see section 9) and pad
T up to the next one; padded rows of x are zero (TMA out-of-bounds fill, or `cp.async` with
src-size 0 as `proj_kernel` does today at `submission.py:240-244`). Padding costs tensor
throughput only, which is free at T <= 128 (section 3.5) and at most 2x waste in a rare test
shape (T = 33 -> 64, T = 72 -> 128). T > 256 (test shape 264, and bf16_proj's 512 and 1000)
stays on cuBLAS.

### 3.2 Tiles, stages, shared memory

BK = 64 (one 128-byte swizzle row per operand row). Per stage: W 64 x 64 x 2 = 8 KB, x
N x 128 B.

| config | tokens N | CTA rows | consumer WGs | acc regs/thread | stage KB (W + x) | stages | smem KB | CTAs/SM |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 8, 16, 32, 64 | 64 | 1 | N/2 (4 to 32) | 8 + 1..8 | 8 | 72 to 128 | 2 (1 at N=64) |
| B | 128 | 64 | 1 | 64 | 8 + 16 = 24 | 6 | 144 + epilogue | 1 |
| C | 256 | 128 | 2 (64 rows each) | 128 | 16 + 32 = 48 | 4 | 192 + epilogue | 1 |

Accumulators: a 64 x N FP32 tile over the 128 threads of a warpgroup is N/2 registers per
thread (CUTLASS `CLayout_64xN` has thread mode 4 x 8 x 4 = 128 and value mode 2 x 2 x N/8 =
N/2, section 9). At N = 256 that is 128 registers; with one producer warp plus two consumer
warpgroups (288 or 384 threads) `__launch_bounds__(384, 1)` leaves 168 registers per thread,
enough for 128 accumulators plus descriptors without `setmaxnreg`. Config C cannot be two
CTAs per SM (smem) and does not need `setmaxnreg`; keep it out of v1.

Bytes in flight per SM: config A with 2 CTAs x 7 stages x 9 to 16 KB = 126 to 224 KB; B: 5 x
24 = 120 KB; C: 3 x 48 = 144 KB. The streaming bench reached its ceiling with 128 KB in
flight per SM (528 x 512 threads x 64 B), so these depths are sufficient. Little's law at
4.05 TB/s / 132 SMs = 31 GB/s per SM and ~2 us loaded latency needs about 62 KB per SM.

x in shared memory across the whole K loop: m = 16 needs 16 x 8192 x 2 = 256 KB, more than
the 227 KB a block may hold, and the per-CTA K-slice of x (m x K/S x 2 = 64 KB at m = 16,
S = 4) would only fit at the cost of the W ring. x streams per stage, as the brief expects.

### 3.3 Weight path: bulk copies of pre-swizzled contiguous tiles, no tensor map

`prepare()` repacks each weight once (as `_pack_mma_a` does now, `submission.py:520-524`)
into [row tile of 64][k tile of 64] chunks of 8 KB, each already in the 128B-swizzle
canonical layout (8-row x 128-byte atoms, 16-byte chunk index XOR row mod 8). The producer
warp then issues one `cp.async.bulk.shared::cluster.global.mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes`
per stage (8 or 16 KB, contiguous), the exact instruction already used in
`muse_moe_w4a16/experiments/tma_and_large_tiles.py:970-975`. Benefits: no
`cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` for the 38 to 67 MB operands, one instruction per stage instead of
512 `cp.async` per stage, and each CTA streams one contiguous region of DRAM (its row tile's
K-slice), which is the access pattern the streaming bench's best grids had.

The wgmma A descriptor for a tile: start address >> 4 in bits 0-13, LBO field ignored for
swizzled K-major layouts (set 1), SBO = 1024 B (>> 4 = 64) between 8-row groups, base offset
0 (tile bases 1024-byte aligned; round the dynamic smem pointer up by hand because the
runtime guarantees only 16 bytes), layout type 1 = 128B swizzle (section 9). Advancing one
k16 step inside a BK = 64 tile adds 32 bytes, i.e. +2 in the start-address field, the same
arithmetic the attention kernel's `desc(ks + 256, ...)` calls use at `submission.py:2636-2637`.

### 3.4 x path: v1 cp.async, v2 TMA with multicast

v1 (configs A and B): the consumer threads copy the x tile (N x 128 B per stage) with 16-byte
`cp.async.cg` into the swizzled layout (chunk ^= row & 7), then `cp.async.wait_group`,
`fence.proxy.async.shared::cta`, and an mbarrier arrive, so the wgmma (async proxy) sees the
generic-proxy writes. This is the fenced pattern the ws attention kernel uses
(`submission.py:2119`, CLAUDE.md rule). At N = 16 it is one `cp.async` per thread per stage.

v2 (config B at m = 128 and config C): x through `cp.async.bulk.tensor.2d` with a tensor map
(box N x 64, SWIZZLE_128B, out-of-bounds rows zero-filled, created per call on the host with
`cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` obtained via `cudaGetDriverEntryPoint`, passed as a
`__grid_constant__` parameter). The reason for v2 is L2 traffic, not DRAM: every CTA
re-reads x's K-slice, so x traffic = (N_rows / CTA rows) x m x K x 2 B. For the pooler that
is 16 MB at m = 16, 32 MB at m = 32, 128 MB at m = 128, 256 MB at m = 256 with 64-row CTAs.
L2-to-SM bandwidth on this part is uncertain: Chips and Cheese measured 5.5 TB/s near-partition
and 3.8 TB/s aggregate on a throttled H100 PCIe; cuBLAS's own m = 128 pooler kernel (64x64
tiles, 24.8 us) moves at least 195 MB through that path, so H200 sustains >= 7.7 TB/s there.
Multicast (`.multicast::cluster` with a 16-bit CTA mask, section 9) across the row tiles of a
cluster divides x traffic by the cluster's row extent. Targets: keep x traffic under ~40 MB
per GEMM.

### 3.5 Grid, split-K and clusters per layer

Rows per 64-row tile: qkv 36, o 128, pooler 64, unpooler 128 (slice: 16). Split-K S is a
cluster along K with a DSMEM reduce of the [64 x N] FP32 partials (at most 64 KB per CTA at
N = 256; 4 KB at N = 16), done exactly as `proj_kernel` does now (`submission.py:402-418`) but
with S <= 4.

| layer (K) | m = 16/32 (config A) | m = 128 (B) | m = 256 (C, 128-row CTAs) |
|---|---|---|---|
| qkv_gate (8192) | 36 tiles x S=4 = 144 CTAs, cluster (1,4) | 36 x S=4 = 144, cluster (2 rows mcast, 4 k) = 8; x traffic 36 MB | 18 x S=8 = 144, cluster (2, 4); x 36 MB |
| o (1024) | 128 x S=1 = 128, no cluster | 128 x 1, cluster (2,1) mcast; x 16 MB | 64 x S=2 = 128, cluster (2,2); x 16 MB |
| pooler (8192) | 64 x S=2 = 128 (or S=4 = 256 at 2 CTAs/SM), cluster (1,2) | 64 x S=2 = 128, cluster (4 rows, 2 k) = 8; x 32 MB | 32 x S=4 = 128, cluster (2,4); x 64 MB |
| unpooler (4096) | 128 x S=1 = 128 (S=2 = 256 at 2/SM) | 128 x 1, cluster (4,1); x 32 MB | 64 x S=2 = 128, cluster (2,2); x 64 MB |
| unpooler slice (4096), T <= 8 | 16 x S=8 = 128, cluster (1,8) | | |
| router hi+lo (2 x 8192) | 4 x S=8 = 32 CTAs (cluster (1,8)), or S=32 with TMA reduce-add | same | same |

All clusters are portable (<= 8). Cluster size 16 (non-portable) would cut the m = 256 x
traffic to 32 MB but needs a whole GPC free, which the side-stream router kernel can deny;
not recommended.

Tensor-core budget (section 9: 989 TFLOPS dense, 1892 FMA/clk/SM at 1.98 GHz):

- m <= 32: a 64 x 16 x 16 wgmma needs 2.5 KB of smem operands per 16k FMA; at 128 B/clk that
  caps the tensor pipe at ~43% of peak, which is still 3.5x more than the K loop needs at the
  memory rate. Memory-bound by a wide margin.
- m = 128: pooler 8.6 GFLOP = 8.7 us at peak, 11.1 us at 78%; under the 17.9 us memory time.
- m = 256: pooler/unpooler 17.2 GFLOP = 17.4 us at peak, 22.3 us at 78%; compute-bound.
  qkv 9.7 GFLOP = 12.5 us at 78%; o 4.3 GFLOP = 5.6 us. Two consumer warpgroups per CTA are
  needed here so one issues wgmma while the other waits on its barrier; smem operand traffic
  is 74 B/clk for the two 64x256 tiles plus 44 B/clk of TMA writes, under 128 B/clk.

Expected kernel times if the kernel reaches t_min (and 78% of tensor peak where that binds):

| m | qkv | o | pooler | unpooler | router hi/lo |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16, 32 | 10.6 | 5.4 | 17.9 | 17.9 | 3.4 |
| 128 | 10.8 | 5.6 | 18.5 | 18.5 | 3.6 |
| 256 | 12.5 to 13 | 6 | 22 to 23 | 22 to 23 | 4 |

Against cuBLAS (standalone kernel us, `docs/hotspots.md`): m=16: 9.9 (two kernels), 4.6,
21.1 (two), 18.5; m=32: 10.5, 4.8, 21.9, 18.9; m=128: 15.3 (two), 5.4, 24.8, 20.5; m=256:
19.4, 8.1, 28.7, 24.9. Per-step kernel savings: m=16 about 4 us plus two fewer launches;
m=32 about 5 plus two launches; m=128 about 10.5 plus one launch; m=256 about 17. The layer
profile's deltas are larger (12.5, 12.7, 21, 27 us) because of the inflation in section 0.

### 3.6 Epilogue and numerics

Each consumer warpgroup writes its 64 x N FP32 tile to shared memory (after the DSMEM
split-K sum when S > 1), converts to BF16 once, and stores `out[t, n0..n0+63]` as 128-byte
rows (16-byte stores, or a TMA 2D store). This is FP32 accumulation across all of K followed
by one rounding, the same contract cuBLAS and today's `store_out` keep. Probe rows (one
power-of-two entry) stay exact in any summation order because every product is exact and the
other terms are zero. The router variant keeps FP32 output.

### 3.7 Pipeline mechanics

Producer warp (one elected lane): for stage s, wait `empty[s]` (parity), `mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx`
with the stage's bytes, issue the W bulk copy (and the x TMA in v2). Consumers: wait
`full[s]`, `wgmma.fence`, four `wgmma` per BK = 64 (one per k16), `wgmma.commit_group`,
`wgmma.wait_group 0` before arriving on `empty[s]`. The attention kernel's comment at
`submission.py:2784-2785` records that leaving a wgmma in flight across the loop back-edge
made ptxas serialize every wgmma (C7514); waiting to zero per stage is the safe default and
costs nothing while memory-bound. In config C (compute-bound) let each warpgroup keep one
stage in flight (`wait_group 1`) and check the ptxas output for that warning.

## 4. Q2: the m = 1 and m = 8 GEMV

### 4.1 What limits proj_kernel today

Nothing inside the kernel that a load path can fix. Its standalone kernel times (10.2, 4.7,
18.2 us) sit on the judge's streaming line `1.3 us + B / 4.05 TB/s` (10.6, 5.4, 17.9). The
runs.md lessons that the brief lists (cluster reduction, cp.async issue, bytes in flight,
pipeline depth) were all measured above 8 tokens; at m = 1 the bench showed the reduction
costing about 1 us (qkv `(1,4,1,8,4,False)` 17.6 vs `(1,8,1,8,4,True)` 18.6 bench us,
`bench.4afc0b73f2a74a69.log`) and nothing else moved it. The two visible inefficiencies:

- The unpooler slice: 4.1 us for 8 MiB against t_min 3.4. Its grid is 16 row tiles x S = 8 =
  128 blocks of 4 warps whose whole K-slice (64 KB) fits in the prologue, so the kernel is
  pure latency: ramp, one burst, an 8-way cluster reduce. About 0.7 us is recoverable with
  256 CTAs (S = 16 is not a portable cluster; use 2 CTAs per SM with 32 KB each and S = 8).
- The per-launch overhead and ramp (judge adds 1.2 to 2.2 us per kernel; the kernel's own
  intercept is ~1.3 us). This is the only lever of size at T <= 8: programmatic dependent
  launch (PDL). Launch each projection with `cudaLaunchAttributeProgrammaticStreamSerialization`
  (the layer already has `launch_pdl`, `submission.py:3719-3731`, captured into graphs as
  `cudaGraphDependencyTypeProgrammatic` edges), issue the first STAGES-1 weight stages before
  `griddepcontrol.wait`, and load x after it. Weights do not depend on the previous kernel, so
  the ring fills during the predecessor's tail. The predecessor must execute
  `griddepcontrol.launch_dependents` early for the overlap to be more than launch latency; our
  attention, finalize and (if X5 is adopted) boundary kernels can, SGLang's norm kernels and
  cuBLAS cannot (then the implicit trigger fires when all primary blocks exit, which still
  removes the launch gap). The W4 port measured "PDL saves 2-4 us per forward"
  (`docs/runs-moe.md`, lessons). Estimate 0.5 to 1.0 us per projection launch, 2 to 4 us per
  step at every T.

So the "85-90%" GEMV design is not available on this judge; the design that is available is
the same TMA + wgmma kernel at N = 8 (configs A with S = 4/8), whose only expected gains over
today are the unpooler slice (~0.7 us) and whatever E1 shows above 4.05 TB/s, plus PDL. If E1
shows the bulk-copy streamer no faster than the plain-load streamer, keep `proj_kernel` at
m <= 8 and add PDL to it (3 to 4 hours, item 3 below).

Register-only GEMV (the brief's "16-byte loads straight to registers, no smem"): workable at
m = 1 (x K-slice of 2048 in registers is 32 regs per lane), but at m = 8 x no longer fits and
the FMAs go back to shared memory at 128 B of x per 16 B of weights, which is the smem-bound
regime runs.md lesson 1 already hit. Tensor cores (N = 8 wgmma or today's mma) are the right
tool at m = 8; there is no bandwidth to gain from the register design at m = 1.

### 4.2 The FP32 router at T <= 8

Why T = 8 is slow (13.5 us in the layer, 7.8 us standalone with BF16 x, 4.4 at T = 1):

1. The kernel is phase-serial: all 8 MB of weights are loaded into registers first
   (`submission.py:93-98`, 32 regs per lane), then x is staged, then the FMA loop runs, then
   the cluster reduce. Nothing overlaps.
2. The FMA loop is shared-memory bound: one 16-byte `LDS` per 4 FMAs per token
   (`submission.py:118-131`), 512 KB of smem reads per block at T = 8 with FP32 x (the layer
   stages FP32, `muse_decode_layer/submission.py:434-470`), about 4096 clocks = 2.1 us at
   128 B/clk, twice the BF16-x version's traffic.
3. In the layer it runs on the side stream concurrently with the pooler
   (`submission.py:4955-4967`), sharing HBM with a 64 MiB stream; its wall time stretches to the
   pooler's pace. The same kernel is 7.8 us standalone.

Fix, if it mattered: register-block x (each lane keeps its 4 k-columns x 8 tokens = 32
FP32 registers) and stream weights row by row from global with 8 x 16-byte loads in flight
per lane, accumulating `acc[rows][8]` and reducing across lanes once per warp; no shared
memory in the loop, loads overlap FMAs, FP32 FMA count unchanged (exact FP32 semantics
kept). Expected ~3.5 to 4 us standalone at T = 8. In the layer it is worth about nothing:
the side chain (router + top-8 + route_align) is already hidden under the pooler at T = 8
(the router port's whole gain at verify 1 came from replacing SGLang's 26 us F.linear,
`docs/runs-decode-layer.md:58`), and the 8 MB it reads cost the pooler the same 2 us either
way. A hi+lo tensor-core split at T <= 8 would need x rounded to BF16 (or a three-term
x_hi/x_lo split); SGLang keeps FP32 activations here, so I do not propose it.

## 5. Q3: the router above 8 tokens

Same kernel, HILO mode as today (`submission.py:272-274`, 317-318): the packed stream
alternates an 8 KB hi tile and an 8 KB lo tile per 64-k step; the producer loads one x tile
per pair; the consumer runs the four wgmma twice (hi then lo) against the same B descriptor
into one FP32 accumulator; FP32 epilogue, no rounding. 256 rows = 4 row tiles, K = 8192, 16
MiB of hi+lo bytes... correction: hi and lo are 256 x 8192 x 2 B each, 8 MiB together.
Parallelism: 4 row tiles x S = 8 = 32 CTAs with a DSMEM reduce (each CTA 256 KB, about
1.3 + 256 KB at ~100 GB/s per SM = 4 us), or S = 32 (128 CTAs, 64 KB each) with
`cp.reduce.async.bulk.tensor ... .add` into a zeroed FP32 [m x 256] buffer (zeroing is a
0.7 us graph node, `docs/runs.md:33`; confirm `.add` with f32 in the PTX ISA table before
relying on it, I could not re-fetch that table). Expected 3.5 to 4.5 us at any m <= 256
against cuBLAS's 9.4 to 12.5 us plus the add and the splitK reduce.

Its value in the layer is indirect: `docs/ruled-out.md:53` shows the router hidden under the
pooler at 9-32 tokens. Once the pooler drops from 20 to 18 us and PDL trims the main chain,
the side chain (router 9.4 + add 1 + reduce 2 + routing 3 + route_align 2, about 17 us at
T = 16, and 12.5 + 19.4 (splitK reduce, 2 calls) at T = 256) becomes the critical path.
Treat it as part of item 1, not a separate gain. The earlier failure at 128/256 tokens
(`docs/ruled-out.md:18`) was per-token-group re-reads of the 8 MB; this kernel reads it once
with N = 128 or 256, so that entry's mechanism does not apply.

## 6. Q4: porting into muse_decode_layer

- T is arbitrary in tests (9, 33, 72, 264 appear in `muse_decode_layer/TASK.md:59-71`). Pad
  N to {8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256}; T > 256 falls back to cuBLAS (`_gemm`); keep the
  `_proj_wins`-style table keyed on T and layer, and route the unpooler at T <= 8 to the
  1024-row slice with S = 8 (the kernel takes `n` as a runtime row count; the packed weight
  holds all 8192 rows and the slice is its first 16 row tiles).
- Inputs must be contiguous [T, K] BF16 with row stride K: `_proj` already calls
  `.contiguous()`; the attention output `o` and `expert_output` come from our kernels. A
  tensor map (v2) bakes x's address at capture; graph replays reuse the captured buffers, as
  every captured kernel argument already assumes.
- Numerics: FP32 accumulate, one BF16 rounding (section 3.6). The split-K sum order differs
  from cuBLAS's; the judge compares against FP64 at 1% / 0.01% (router), and probe rows stay
  exact. Keep the self-tests at `submission.py:551-568` (relative L2 plus `torch.equal` on the
  probe row) and add T in {9, 16, 33, 72, 128, 256, 264}.
- Shared memory: dynamic smem base must be rounded up to 1024 bytes for the 128B swizzle;
  configs B/C need `cudaFuncAttributeMaxDynamicSharedMemorySize` above 144 KB; mbarriers in
  static smem.
- Clusters and the side stream: cluster launches need co-resident SMs in one GPC; the router
  kernel on the side stream occupies up to 32 SMs. Keep clusters <= 8 and 128 to 144 CTAs per
  GEMM; if E3 shows cluster waits, use S = 1 with 2 CTAs per SM where the row count allows.
- PDL ordering: `griddepcontrol.wait` must precede the first read of x and the first write of
  `out`; weights may be prefetched before it. On the side stream the router kernel's
  predecessor is the boundary kernel (SGLang's at T > 8), so only the implicit trigger
  applies there.
- Compile budget: prepare() is at 98.8 s of 300 (`docs/runs-decode-layer.md:68`); the W4
  extension alone took 46.8 s. Keep the new kernel to about 12 instantiations (6 N values x
  {bf16 out, f32 out} with ROWS and S as runtime or few-valued template parameters) and build
  it as its own extension so a failure falls back cleanly, as `_try` does today.
- Environmental slowdown: the layer profile shows our o kernel at 6.9 us (4.7 standalone) and
  cuBLAS's o at 7.2 (4.2). Part is profiler inflation (section 0), part may be real. A new
  kernel inherits whatever is real; only overlap (PDL) attacks it.

## 9. Hardware and ISA facts relied on

- H200 SXM: 4.8 TB/s HBM3e, 141 GB, 1,979 BF16 TFLOPS with sparsity (989 dense), 67 FP32
  TFLOPS (nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h200). 132 SMs and ~1.98 GHz boost are the GH100 SXM
  figures; 989e12 / (132 x 1.98e9) = 3784 FLOP/clk/SM = 1892 FMA/clk/SM.
- Hopper SM (CUDA Hopper tuning guide): 228 KB shared memory per SM, 227 KB per block,
  64K 32-bit registers per SM, 255 per thread, 50 MB L2 in two partitions, TMA moves 1D to
  5D tensors global<->shared and between cluster CTAs' shared memory, portable cluster size
  8 (16 non-portable with `cudaFuncAttributeNonPortableClusterSizeAllowed`), DSMEM reads,
  writes and atomics across a cluster.
- wgmma (CUTLASS `cute/atom/mma_traits_sm90_gmma.hpp` and `cute/arch/mma_sm90_gmma.hpp`,
  fetched): `CLayout_64xN = Layout<Shape<Shape<_4,_8,_4>, Shape<_2,_2,Int<N/8>>>, ...>`, i.e.
  128 threads x N/2 values; BF16 x BF16 -> F32 atoms instantiated for N = 8, 16, 32, 64, 96,
  128, 192, 256 (`MMA_64xNx16_F32BF16BF16_SS`, A and B from smem descriptors, and `_RS` with A
  in registers; B is always smem). The PTX ISA's shape table allows every multiple of 8 for
  16-bit inputs; I could not re-fetch that page (the fetch tool truncates it and the PDF is
  over its size limit), and the design uses only the instantiated set. Operand constraints
  in the atom: accumulators `"+f"`, descriptors `"l"`, scale/transpose flags `"n"`, scale_D
  via a predicate. `wgmma.fence.sync.aligned`, `wgmma.commit_group.sync.aligned`,
  `wgmma.wait_group.sync.aligned N` are already wrapped at
  `muse_decode_layer/submission.py:2133-2142`.
- Shared-memory matrix descriptor (`cute/arch/mma_sm90_desc.hpp`, fetched): start address
  bits [0,14) (>> 4), leading byte offset [16,30) (>> 4, ignored for swizzled layouts),
  stride byte offset [32,46) (>> 4), base offset [49,52), layout type [62,64) with
  SWIZZLE_NONE 0, 128B 1, 64B 2, 32B 3. K-major SW128 atom: 8 rows x 1024 bits = 8 x 64 BF16,
  `Swizzle<3,4,3>`.
- TMA / bulk copy instruction text (`cute/arch/copy_sm90_tma.hpp`, fetched):
  `cp.async.bulk.tensor.2d.shared::cluster.global.mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes.L2::cache_hint [dst], [map, {c0, c1}], [mbar], hint;`
  multicast form adds `.multicast::cluster` and a 16-bit `"h"` CTA mask;
  `cp.reduce.async.bulk.tensor.2d.global.shared::cta.add.bulk_group [map, {c0, c1}], [src];`
  `cp.async.bulk.shared::cluster.global.mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes [dst], [src], bytes, [mbar];`
  fences `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta`, `cp.async.bulk.commit_group`,
  `cp.async.bulk.wait_group.read N`. In-repo use: `muse_moe_w4a16/experiments/tma_and_large_tiles.py:948-975`.
- `setmaxnreg.inc/dec.sync.aligned.u32 N` (`cutlass/arch/reg_reconfig.h`, fetched; compiled
  only for sm_90a). Not needed by the proposed configs.
- PDL (CUDA programming guide 4.5, fetched): `cudaGridDependencySynchronize` blocks until the
  primaries "have completed and flushed results to global memory"; if the primary never calls
  the trigger "it implicitly occurs after all thread blocks in the primary kernel exit";
  stream capture with `programmaticStreamSerializationAllowed = 1` records a
  `cudaGraphDependencyTypeProgrammatic` edge; concurrency "is opportunistic and not
  guaranteed". In-repo: `muse_decode_layer/submission.py:3307-3308, 3719-3731`.
- L2 bandwidth: Chips and Cheese, H100 PCIe (throttled to ~1.4 GHz), over 5.5 TB/s near
  partition, 3.8 TB/s across the full 50 MB; no SXM/H200 measurement found. cuBLAS's m = 128
  pooler kernel implies >= 7.7 TB/s on this judge (section 3.4).
- Streaming ceiling on this judge: `docs/runs-moe.md:24`, kernel `tools/moe_make_bench.py:27-60`.

### 4.1 vjeux/okc-2026 and Madhavan113/kerneloptimizer (the strongest open code)

- https://github.com/vjeux/okc-2026 ("team vjeux", Apache 2.0, created 2026-10-27): five complete single-file CUDA submissions (attention 154 KB, proj 189 KB, layer 569 KB, MoE 179 KB, prefill 292 KB). The README states only the structure; the file docstrings describe the designs. Official API rows for vjeux: 1.501 / 2.610 / 2.327 / 2.102 / 1.798 (per-board ranks 169 / 39 / 72 / 75 / 39); Madhavan113: 1.493 / 2.588 / 2.332 / 2.101 / 1.796 (ranks 181 / 52 / 60 / 76 / 40).
- https://github.com/Madhavan113/kerneloptimizer: `notes/pub_moe_design.md`, `pub_attention_design.md`, `pub_proj_design.md` are line-referenced reverse-engineering memos of the vjeux files ("Reference design only: re-implement"), and `notes/decode_layer_map.md` and `notes/skx_streamk.md` are Madhavan113's own judged experiments. Madhavan113's stored runs (states): attention 2.5883x (job 26c40f28a3f74b2a), MoE 2.3318x (080c57e6047b4794), proj 1.4933x (8bd137632d7a4cc5), layer 2.0762x (711bbae5d04143b3) and later 2.1112x (b73aff83), prefill 1.7960x (45ca53d9449b4d00). The decode-layer map says the layer embeds the vjeux attention and MoE CUDA byte-for-byte and a forked proj module, so the two repos describe one kernel family (inferred from the memo's "BYTE-IDENTICAL" diffs).

MoE (`pub_moe_design.md`, memo header "2.32x vs SGLang Marlin on H200"; states):
- One kernel launch per call: routing prologue run redundantly by every CTA, GEMM1 + SwiGLU, GEMM2 + norm statistics, a software grid barrier, then the final norm and weighted sum. Grid = SM count (132), one CTA per SM, no PDL ("one launch per call gains nothing").
- Four compiled variants by M: TINY (M ≤ 4), TINY2 (5-8), MID (9-16): `mma.sync.m16n8k16` "skinny" units of 16 weight rows × full K with 8 compute warps splitting K (512 each) plus a helper warp for epilogues; MAIN (M ≥ 17): RS-wgmma `m64nNk16` with A = dequantized weights in registers, B = gathered x in shared memory, N = 8 × ceil(tokens/8) up to 64, 4 consumer warpgroups + 2 TMA producer warps, stream-K over 256-K stages with cost tables.
- Weights stream by TMA bulk copies of 36,864 B units (one 16-row × 4096-K block including scales), 3-slot ring; x goes global to registers for the skinny path. Hot experts: an expert with more than 8 tokens becomes ceil(tot/64) "fat" jobs of ≤ 64 tokens, listed first, largest first; in MID, experts with more than 8 tokens are split into ≤ 8-token jobs (weights re-streamed).
- Dequant: "7 ALU + 2 IMAD.SHL per 8 weights" (mask M = 0x81C081C0, shifts and funnel shifts chosen so a bit permutation done once in `prepare()` lands E2M1 bits in BF16 positions as value × 2^-126), scale built with PRMT + IMAD (+0x5C005C00) and applied with one HMUL2 per word; global scale in the epilogue as gs × 2^62.
- GEMM1 to GEMM2 chaining through global memory with `evict_last` hints; per-job readiness flags (`doneA`); in WGS the phase-A epilogue writes straight into phase-B's wgmma B layout. L2 prefetch of every x row (`prefetch.global.L2`) at kernel start; the first two unit TMAs are issued before routing ("off the cold-start critical path").
- Recorded deltas: "bs1 +2.5% / +3.5%" (FINPF), "bs8 +2.0..2.5%", stream-K cost table "bs32 +0.45, bs128 +0.94, bs256 +0.17%".

Attention (`pub_attention_design.md`, "check 2.58x vs SGLang FA3"; states):
- One launch per call, no memset, no second pass. Splits never exchange a running max: each split adds o·2^m and l·2^m into an FP32 workspace with `red.global.add.v4.f32` (QK-norm bounds the logits), and the last CTA (a ticket counting keys) or every CTA (cooperative finalize) normalizes, applies RMSNorm × sigmoid(gate), and zeroes what it read.
- Two kernel families: per-request split-KV, grid (n_splits, B, Hkv/2), for sliding windows and single requests; a "flat" kernel, grid (264,1,1) = 2 CTAs/SM, for full context at B > 1, where all requests' keys are split into equal shares with a per-boundary penalty (SEGK 400 for q1, 600 for q8: "b16 107.4 -> 103, b32 187.4 -> 184") and a producer warpgroup (setmaxnreg 56/200 at q1, 32/104 at q8) feeding a 3- or 4-stage mbarrier ring.
- One CTA = one request × one KV pair (16 query heads); a 128-byte cache row holds both KV heads and is fetched once as 8 × 16-byte `cp.async.cg`. 64-key tiles in 128B-swizzled smem that doubles as the wgmma B descriptor.
- q1: f16 `mma.sync` with E4M3 → f16 converted in registers (no FP8 MMA). q8: FP8 wgmma for QK^T (m64n64k32) and PV (m64n72k32) with eight rows of E4M3 ones in V^T that produce the row sums for free; lazy softmax offset checked with a bit test on packed P bytes.
- Latency work on sliding shapes: seq_len speculated from the page-table width at B = 1 and verified after the index group lands (SPEC), K/V issued as soon as page indices land, straight-line predicated copies, magic-multiplier division, cooperative finalize. Per-shape plans: decode 1 sliding 32 CTAs with one 64-key tile each ("6.6 -> 6.5 us vs 32" splits), verify 1 sliding 33 CTAs ("coop beats clusters 13.0 -> 10.2 us"), verify 32 sliding "4 splits per request, 128 CTAs one per SM, 16.10 -> 15.50", full B = 1 252 splits with 8 workspace copies ("coop with 1/2/4 copies +26/+16/+4%: same-address red serialization of 250 splits").
- Things that lost: "FMA-pipe exponentials", "two streams per CTA", "sense-reversing barriers", TMA for q8 page indices (+0.7%), PDL on the standalone (~0.3% worse).

Projections (`pub_proj_design.md`, "1.50x vs SGLang"; states):
- Lossless 12-bit weights for m ≤ 32: low byte raw, 4-bit code for the high byte as an offset in an 8-value exponent window chosen per matrix; escapes (weights outside the window) applied by dedicated escape warps from a per-CTA table while the weights stream; decode is about 12 integer ops per 8 weights.
- `sk2` kernel for m = 8/16/32: x is the mma A operand (16 tokens), weights the B operand (8 rows); no cross-CTA split-K (K is split only across warps inside the CTA); weights by one bulk copy per stage (12-24 KB), x by a 3-D TMA box; 96-256 CTAs, 3-6 stages, 64-213 KB smem per config. The router at m ≤ 32 uses a 3-CTA cluster with a DSMEM reduction.
- m = 1 is autotuned among a 12-bit CUDA-core GEMV (`cgemv`, "pooler m1 2x512 -0.34 us vs sk2"), `sgemv`, `rgemv` (FP32 router), `sk2`, cuBLAS. m = 128/256 never uses 12-bit ("the wide (RS-wgmma) kernel never beats cuBLAS for BF16 m 33..256"): cuBLAS, cuBLAS on a K-major copy, cluster split-K kernels `gq`/`gqx` ("cuBLAS 16.4 -> 14.0 us" at qkv m128), CUTLASS pingpong 128x64x64 for pooler m256 ("31.3 vs 34.5 raw").
- `prepare()` autotunes every (layer, m) with CUDA-graph capture, a 256 MB cold-L2 sweep before each replay, 24 interleaved reps, and an FP64 self-test gate.

Decode layer (`decode_layer_map.md`; states, judged 2.092x at job f662ee18, later 2.1112x):
- At T ≤ 32, nine launches, all with PDL: qkv `sk2` → attention → o `sk2` → `_boundary1` (Triton, one program per token) → fused pooler + router `sk2f` (T 1/8/16; separate at T = 32) → `_route_split` → `moe_fused` (one launch) → unpooler `sk2` → `_boundary2`. At T > 32 (verify 16/32) cuBLAS for every dense GEMM, pooler + router as one `torch.mm` on a concatenated [4608 × 8192] weight, no PDL ("-1% at T = 256").
- Budget at decode 1 sliding (judged 77.1 µs): attention 4.9, MoE 36.7, dense GEMMs 39.3 (qkv 10.1 / o 5.8 / pooler+router 17.7 / unpooler 5.7), glue 13.2 (three Triton kernels, "8-17% of the judged time").
- Negative results, all judged: fusing the glue into a last-CTA tail of the GEMV ("o launch 9.0 -> 49.2 us", "LATENCY-BOUND"); a boundary prologue recomputing the norm in every CTA (+13.3 µs at T = 1); "under PDL a kernel must not end with a grid barrier (it blocks the dependent's early start: 3-5 us)"; "PDL depth 2 = 3 = 4 = 6 at every T"; routing fused into the pooler kernel (2.051, regression); the standalone proj module composed into the layer lost on every T ≤ 32 shape; attention `-DOKC_PDLKV=1` +0.4..+1.1 µs. "MoE and attention kernel times move 5-20 us run to run on identical code" because the judge's fresh routing differs per run.
- `skx_streamk.md`: a persistent stream-K wgmma GEMM for m = 128/256 lost to cuBLAS/`gqx` in four judged checks (1.4756, 1.4620, 1.4781, 1.4882 vs 1.4933 reference). Attribution: the main loop alone beats the picks by 1.2-1.6 µs (W streams at 4.1-4.2 TB/s plus ~2 µs ramp), and any global fixup costs 9-11 µs. "No stream-K / global-fixup form wins at m=128 on this GPU; the gqx / gq cluster-DSMEM forms win precisely because they have no global fixup."
- `codex-research-handoff.md` lists what the team considers already done (persistent execution, TMA, WGMMA, stream-K, lossless packing, PDL) and the remaining bets (a verify-GEMM decomposition experiment, distributing paged-KV address math across lanes, MoE weight-stream dependencies, Cohere-style dependency-driven persistent layer as a research branch).

## 6. Cross-source synthesis per topic

Decode-layer structure. Nobody shipped a megakernel: vjeux/Madhavan113 run nine PDL-chained launches at T ≤ 32 (states), lee101 11 per load (states), infraax 16-20 (states), operatorstack keeps SGLang's structure with per-token-count kernel swaps (states); infraax lists a "single-launch megakernel" among closed ideas and Madhavan113 lists Cohere's megakernel as a research branch, so a true megakernel is unproven here (inferred). Fusing the small glue kernels into neighbouring GEMVs lost in three independent attempts (Madhavan113 last-CTA tails, lee101 v31 epilogues, infraax grid-barrier fusion) and the one measured glue win is a side stream for the router over the pooler (SGLang's own structure). The MoE is the largest block at every decode shape and the attention at full-context batch 16/32 (every profile agrees).

MoE GEMM. Every open design puts weights on the MMA M side (register A operand after in-register dequant) and tokens on N: vjeux `mma.sync` 16-row units with K split across 8 warps for ≤ 16 tokens and RS-wgmma `m64nNk16` with N ≤ 64 and stream-K above (states); lee101 persistent `mma.sync` with TMA rings and heaviest-first queue (states); operatorstack `mma_v2` register-A with per-item 8/16/32-row tiles (states); a wgmma shared-B path "was off, because the register path was faster" (operatorstack states). Dequant cost is the agreed lever: Marlin 15+4 ops per 8 values, vjeux 7+2 integer plus 4 HMUL2, lee101 8 integer plus 4 HMUL2 (states); lee101 and arkintof both report that cutting instructions without keeping occupancy gains nothing (states). Hot experts are handled by chunking (vjeux fat jobs ≤ 64 tokens; operatorstack 32-row items; Ranoobaba Marlin block 16) rather than special kernels; arkintof's hot/cold split was flat (states). Warp-specialised producer/consumer rings lost for lee101 (v6) and infraax (three readings) (states). The leader's 2.62-2.69 is consistent with ~92% of the weight-streaming floor on every load (lee101's inference from floors).

Attention. All open kernels gather page-size-1 FP8 rows as 128-byte rows with 8 lanes × 16 B `cp.async` (vjeux, operatorstack, lee101 states); per-row bulk TMA and one-row-per-thread lose badly (lee101, emeraldant states). Split-KV with a merge: vjeux merges in an absolute frame with FP32 `red.add` and a key-count ticket (states); operatorstack and infraax merge with log-sum-exp by the last program (states). q8 verify blocks use 64-row wgmma tiles (8 tokens × 8 heads) with FP8 QK and FP8 PV (vjeux, lee101 states; operatorstack uses `warpgroup_mma`). Batch-1 sliding shapes are latency chains of 5-6 dependent DRAM trips (Ranoobaba, lee101 states); the fixes that measured were seq-length speculation, issuing K/V as soon as indices land, one 64-key tile per CTA, cooperative finalize (vjeux), and 16-CTA clusters launched with PDL (lee101 s1k 7.2 µs at decode-1 sliding). Clusters larger than 2-4 CTAs fail on GPC packing for big grids (lee101 states). exp2/MUFU is not the verify bottleneck (infraax measured 7%); BN 128 tiles at batch ≥ 16 gave ×1.13-1.16 (infraax states).

Projections. The leaders are inferred (lee101) to sit within ~1.5 µs of a lossless-compressed streaming floor on m ≤ 32 and to beat cuBLAS at m128 with compressed weights; the open code does this with 12-bit lossless weights (vjeux, lee101), swap-AB skinny kernels with no cross-CTA split-K (vjeux sk2), DSMEM cluster reductions where split-K is needed (vjeux router, operatorstack qkv/unpooler), CUDA-core GEMVs at m = 1 (vjeux, operatorstack, bra1nDump), and cuBLAS/CUTLASS at m ≥ 128 (vjeux, Madhavan113, operatorstack). Global split-K fixups cost 4-11 µs and lost everywhere they were tried at m = 128 (Madhavan113 skx, tommyyliu, ozgureyilmaz v028). The router hi/lo split with FP32 accumulation is universally used above 8 tokens; exact FP32 register-accumulated GEMVs win at m ≤ 8 (ozgureyilmaz, vjeux rgemv).

Small-batch latency tricks. PDL: vjeux's layer launches everything with PDL at T ≤ 32 (states); operatorstack chains router partials → reduce and prefetches weights into L2 before `griddepcontrol.wait` (states); bra1nDump measured +4-9% on router split-K pairs (states); infraax measured PDL as noise on Triton kernels, light prefetch +2 µs and full prefetch −3.9 µs at T = 1 (states); Madhavan113 found PDL depth irrelevant and a grid barrier at the end of a PDL-chained kernel costing 3-5 µs (states). L2 prefetch of activations (vjeux XPF2) and issuing the first weight TMAs before routing (vjeux FAST1) measured +2.5-3.5% at bs1 (states); L2 prefetch of KV ahead of the ring hurts (lee101, infraax states). Streams: a side stream for router + routing overlapping the pooler (SGLang baseline, operatorstack, vjeux prefill) is the only stream overlap reported to help; two streams per attention CTA lost (vjeux states). Judge arithmetic that matters for latency: ~4 µs replay cost subtracted, kernels plus inter-kernel gaps of 0.3-0.8 µs are scored, ~2-2.5 µs extra non-kernel gap on cuBLAS-served shapes, and ~3% run-to-run drift (infraax, prateekm1007 states).

# Context: what this repo is for and what we know so far

Written 2026-10-27 from two earlier chats (one with Claude, one with ChatGPT) about the
[Open Kernel Challenge](https://openkernelchallenge.dev), plus the task files `okc init` wrote.

- Claude chat: https://claude.ai/share/0d838d06-5c71-4ffd-ad81-b89f7869cd86
- Claude's field guide: https://claude.ai/artifact/DRUUXPVgr7v5A2HcLyZ8TA
- ChatGPT chat: https://chatgpt.com/share/6ae13c1f-5170-83e8-9529-3dd09b85caa3 (its HTML guide,
  `open_kernel_challenge_guide.html`, only opens inside ChatGPT, so it could not be read here)

## Goal

Get a submission that beats SGLang's baseline (score above 1.00x). The top of the board is not
the goal.

## The challenge

Meta released Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter mixture-of-experts model. The challenge asks
for faster GPU code to run it on NVIDIA H200s. There are two tracks:

- **Kernel track** (Oct 22 to Nov 4, 11:59 pm PT). There are five problems, and each one is a
  single Python file with a `kernel_fn`. Each is timed against the kernel SGLang calls for the
  same step. It has no prizes, but the top 50 on the overall kernel board get priority in the
  serving queue.
- **Serving track** (Nov 5 to Nov 19). Contestants patch SGLang itself, and runs are scored on
  a full 8xH200 node. This is the track with the prizes.

## Concepts, in the order they came up

- **Kernel.** A kernel is one function that runs on the GPU, written in CUDA (NVIDIA's C++
  dialect) or Triton (a Python-based language). Kernels compute every number the model
  produces. A faster kernel computes the same math, equal within rounding, in less time. The
  judge rejects any output that drifts past a small tolerance from an FP64 reference.
- **Where kernels run.** Tokenizing the prompt runs on the CPU. Prefill then runs every prompt
  token through all 62 layers at once. Decode follows, with one step per generated token, and
  each step is a full pass through every layer. A layer is about a dozen kernel launches, so
  one decode step is roughly 800 launches. SGLang batches users together, so one decode step
  might process 1, 16 or 32 users' tokens; these are the "decode 1/16/32" loads.
- **SGLang.** SGLang is the open-source serving engine. It batches requests, manages the KV
  cache and launches kernels, mostly calling libraries: cuBLAS, FlashAttention 3, Marlin.
  `baseline.py` in each problem is exactly SGLang's call sequence. The task is to replace a
  piece of SGLang, not all of it.
- **The floor.** Every shape's time is bounded below by the larger of two figures: the bytes it
  moves divided by 4.8 TB/s, or the FLOPs it does divided by 989 TFLOP/s. Decode shapes are
  memory-bound, so the way to win is to read the weights once at full bandwidth with few
  launches. `TASK.md` prints the floor for every shape.
- **Speculative decoding ("verify").** A draft model guesses 8 tokens and the big model checks
  them all in one step, so verify 16 processes 16 users x 8 tokens = 128 tokens.

## What is unusual about Muse

The model has 256 experts with top-8 routing. It shrinks the hidden vector from 8192 to 4096
around the experts (the pooler and unpooler). Its router is FP32. Its attention is gated, and
46 of the 62 layers use a sliding 2048-token window while 16 attend to the full context. The
expert weights are NVFP4, which the H200 has to unpack to BF16 in software.

## Rules that matter for code

- `kernel_fn` is captured as a CUDA graph. It must not sync with the host (`.item()`,
  `.cpu()`, printing a tensor), and it must not branch on input values. Branching on shapes
  is fine.
- `prepare(weights)` runs once, untimed, for up to 300 s. Compiling and repacking belong there.
- Weights stay at their own precision. The one exception is the FP32 router, which may be
  split into a BF16 hi + lo pair with FP32 accumulation.
- The router tolerance is 0.01% relative L2. About one row in eight of `x` is a single power
  of two (a probe row), and its output must be exact to within 0.1%.
- Native CUDA is allowed through `torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline`, and the rules page
  says so explicitly.
- The daily limits are 10 scored runs and 20 check runs per problem, reset at 00:00 UTC. A run
  has 10 minutes in total, compiling included.
- `okc login` must be run by a person, because it accepts the rules.

1. Where the time goes, shape by shape

Twelve scored shapes, each with our bar above the public entry's. Bar length is the judged time; the segments are each profile's kernel rows grouped by component and scaled to that total, because under programmatic dependent launch the rows overlap and add up to more than the step. Sliding-window shapes count 46 times per step, full-context shapes 16 times, so the top of each pair matters most.

2. One decode token, sliding layer: the launch chain

Each box is one kernel launch, drawn to its profile time; a thin gap is a dependent launch the GPU must wait for; a chevron into a box means that kernel was launched early by programmatic dependent launch (PDL) and only waits for the data it reads. Our router chain runs on a second stream under the pooler. Theirs runs one stream and chains every kernel.

3. What is built differently inside each piece

Three mechanisms account for most of the kernel-level gap. In each panel the left half is ours, the right half the public entry; the colored element is the part that changes.

Attention: how splits are merged

weight-46 shapes: 14.5 µs vs 4.9 µs at decode 1

Ours exchanges a running max through partial buffers and merges in a second launch (or a cluster barrier on sliding layers). Theirs never exchanges a max: QK-norm bounds every logit, so 2^score stays in FP32 range and every split adds straight into one workspace with atomics. No combine launch, no memset, and at batch 1 a plan of 32 CTAs with one 64-key tile each.

MoE: how the expert GEMMs are scheduled

verify 32 sliding: 381 µs vs 198 µs of MoE rows

At 128 and 256 tokens our kernel is bound by traffic between L2 and the SMs: each weight byte crosses 1.5 times because a hot expert is split into 8 to 16-token items, and mma.sync cannot take larger tiles without saturating the shared-memory port. Register-A wgmma, with the dequantized weights in registers and tokens read through a descriptor, takes 64-token jobs. At one to eight tokens the public kernel saves the three launch hops and the fill and drain of four grids.

Dense projections: who reduces, and how many bytes

decode 16: 74 µs vs 51 µs of dense rows

Our single-token GEMVs already sit on the judge's streaming line (1.3 µs plus bytes at 4.05 TB/s), so the public entry's smaller numbers come from moving 25% fewer bytes, not from a better load path. Above eight tokens the difference is one launch instead of two and no reduction across CTAs. Above 32 tokens both entries keep cuBLAS.

# Gap analysis: our decode layer (1.403x) against the public 2.1x entry

Written 2026-10-28. The public entry is https://github.com/vjeux/okc-2026 (Apache-2.0, five
single-file CUDA submissions; official rows 1.501 / 2.610 / 2.327 / 2.102 / 1.798 on proj /
attention / MoE / layer / prefill). A second account, Madhavan113, ships the same kernels
(byte-identical CUDA per its own diff) and published line-referenced design memos plus its
judged layer A/Bs at https://github.com/Madhavan113/kerneloptimizer (`notes/`). Its best judged
layer run is 2.111x (job b73aff83). "Their" numbers below come from those memos, mainly the
judged profile of job f662ee18 (2.092x); ours from job 0e28c26271c94570 (1.403x). Both profiles
run under programmatic dependent launch (PDL), so per-kernel rows include waiting on the kernel
before them and overstate the later kernels on both sides by similar amounts. Where I infer
rather than read, I say so. Copies of the public sources and memos are in this session's
scratchpad (`audit/raw/vjeux/`, `audit/raw/gh4/`); nothing from them is in this repo.

## 1. The four answers

**What was missing.** Not tuning, structure. On every shape our time is the same kernels in the
same arrangement as SGLang's call sequence, with each piece replaced by a faster piece. Their
layer is a different arrangement: 9 launches instead of our 17-23, every launch chained with
PDL instead of only our four MoE kernels, attention and MoE as one launch each with the merge
and the reduction inside the kernel, and the dense projections on a kernel that never reduces
across CTAs. The per-shape table in section 2 puts about 40 us of the 40 us gap at decode 1 on
attention (10 us), launches and glue (about 20 us) and the dense GEMVs (4-8 us); on the verify
shapes the MoE kernel accounts for 85-180 us of the gap and the q_len 8 full-context attention
for 80-170 us.

**What we could have done.** Six decisions, in the order they would have paid (section 4):
(1) build the attention merge in a fixed frame so splits add into an FP32 workspace with
atomics and the last CTA finalizes, which deletes the combine launch and the cross-split max
exchange; (2) launch every kernel of the layer with PDL and issue weight loads before
`griddepcontrol.wait`; (3) replace torch's and SGLang's glue with three one-program-per-token
kernels and drop the side stream; (4) make the MoE one persistent launch with routing done
redundantly by every CTA, TMA bulk copies of whole 36 KB weight units, and a register-A wgmma
path above 16 tokens; (5) put the dense projections on a swap-AB kernel with x as the mma A
operand, weights as B, split-K only across warps, and 12-bit lossless weights whose escapes are
applied by dedicated warps; (6) treat cold code as a cost on the sliding shapes.

**Would our path have arrived?** No. Our last two days of experiments were tuning inside fixed
structures (variant bits, loader arithmetic, K-split counts, layouts, a boundary kernel) and
the score moved +0.02 per day at the end, with nine consecutive MoE and attention checks inside
the judge's confidence interval. The four component audits of today put everything still on
that path at about 1.55-1.65x: the orchestration items +0.10-0.12, the cheap MoE items +0.03,
the attention diet +0.05. The remaining 0.5x is the three structural rewrites above, which were
not on our roadmap except as backlog entries (A3 in-kernel merge, M1 large tiles) that we had
either deferred or ruled out on evidence from the old structure.

**Was the public entry doing something we completely missed?** Yes, several things (section 5):
the fixed-frame softmax merge justified by the QK-norm bound; speculating the sequence length
from the page table's width; a "flat" full-context kernel that gives every CTA an equal share
of all requests' keys; FP8 wgmma for P.V with eight rows of ones in V^T that produce the row
sums for free; register-A wgmma (`wgmma` with A in registers) so a MoE job can have up to 64
tokens without the shared-memory operand traffic that killed our large tiles; weight streaming
by one bulk copy per unit consumed through registers, not through an smem pipeline feeding
mma.sync; escape warps for lossless compression; and a prepare-time tuner that times whole
candidate chains in the layer and pins picks per token count.

| launches per call | route_align (side stream), GEMM1, SwiGLU reduce, GEMM2, finalize: 4 on the main stream, PDL between them | 1: routing prologue run redundantly by every CTA, GEMM1 + SwiGLU, GEMM2 + norm statistics, a software grid barrier, the final norm and weighted sum; counters reset themselves |
| grid | thousands of short blocks (41K launched at T = 256 of which 9.6K work), 4-6 blocks per SM | 132 persistent CTAs, one per SM, static equal slices of the unit list per phase, stream-K with cost tables above 16 tokens |
| weight loads | per-lane 16 B loads straight to registers, a 1 KB stage per warp, 4 stages ahead | one `cp.async.bulk` of a whole 36,864 B unit (16 rows x 4096 K with scales) into a 3-slot ring; the first two units issued before routing starts |
| tokens per weight dequant | 8 or 16 (NT1 / NT2 items); above that the shared-memory port saturates on B fragments, which is why our 64-token tiles lost 2x | up to 8 on mma.sync below 17 tokens; up to 64 on `wgmma m64nNk16` with A (the dequantized weights) in registers and x in smem through a descriptor, above 16 tokens |
| K split | 2-4 across blocks, FP32 partials through HBM (50 MB written and read back at T = 256), reduced by the SwiGLU kernel and the finalizer | across the 8 warps of a CTA with an smem reduction (small T); stream-K across CTAs with a global fixup only for the units cut between CTAs (large T) |
| GEMM1 to GEMM2 | bf16 `inter` through global memory, two launches apart | bf16 `inter` with an evict_last hint and per-job readiness flags; above 16 tokens the GEMM1 epilogue writes straight into GEMM2's wgmma B layout |
| dequant | 14 SASS per 32-bit word (8 weights), 9 on the integer pipe, scale by PRMT + IMAD (the same 2^119 trick) | 7 ALU + 2 IMAD on the FMA pipe per word, one scale PRMT + IMAD per four words thanks to a K permutation that puts one 16-K scale block on one lane's four k-steps |
| x operand | staged in smem per block (32 KB per 16-row item at S = 4), read by ldmatrix | kept in registers for the whole job (16 uint4 per lane), pulled into L2 by `prefetch.global.L2` at kernel start |
| result | 1.699x standalone; at bs 8-32 within 85-97% of the streaming ceiling, at bs 128/256 bound by L2-to-SM traffic at 4.1-4.5 TB/s (today's MoE audit) | 2.327x standalone; MoE rows 60 / 86 us at decode 16 / 32 sliding against our 112 / 120 |

Where our experiments touched theirs and stopped short: our TMA weight kernel (M2) fed a
smem pipeline consumed by mma.sync and lost 3-11% at small T; theirs issues the same bulk
copies but each warp pulls its fragments from the ring into registers and the only per-unit
synchronization is one CTA barrier. Our large-tile kernel (M1) kept mma.sync and put 64
tokens through ldmatrix, which the MoE audit shows saturates the shared-memory port; theirs
uses register-A wgmma, whose B operand goes through the tensor core's own path. Our persistent
kernel walked (item, chunk, split) units and tied the non-persistent one because it kept the
four-launch structure; theirs is persistent to remove launches and to overlap the two GEMMs.

### 3.3 Dense projections

| | ours | theirs |
|---|---|---|
| m = 1 | mma.sync kernel with a 4-stage cp.async ring and a cluster split-K reduction; 65-72% of HBM peak on the big matrices, 32-51% on the small ones | CUDA-core GEMV on 12-bit weights (`cgemv`), `__ldg` straight to registers with every load issued before the first FMA; autotuned against an sk2 config and cuBLAS; 9.2 / 5.2 / 13.7 / 3.5 us for qkv / o / pooler / unpooler slice in the layer |
| m = 8-32 | our kernel only where it won at m = 8 (all but o), cuBLAS above | `sk2`: x is the mma A operand (16 tokens), weights the B operand (8 rows per tile); each CTA owns R rows over the whole K; K split only across the warps of the CTA and reduced through the dead ring; weights by one bulk copy per stage, x by a 3-D TMA box on the same mbarrier; 96-256 CTAs, 1-2 per SM; no cross-CTA reduction at all |
| compression | 12-bit lossless code built, won only on the pooler because the escape-tile lookup sat on the critical path; left out | 12-bit lossless with the same high-byte window idea; escapes applied by 3-4 dedicated warps that take turns on stages, with private accumulators and an uncapped per-CTA table arriving by one bulk copy; the qkv rows are permuted to balance escapes across row blocks |
| router | FP32 CUDA-core kernel at m <= 8 (5.2 / 13.5 us in the layer at T = 1 / 8); cuBLAS hi/lo above | FP32 GEMV `rgemv` at m = 1; sk2 with hi and lo tiles into alternating accumulators and a 3-CTA cluster DSMEM reduction at m = 8-32; fused into the pooler kernel's ring at T = 1-16 (`sk2f`, one launch for pooler + router) |
| m = 128 / 256 | cuBLAS | cuBLAS, plus a 2-3 CTA cluster split-K kernel for qkv at m = 128 (16.4 to 14.0 us) and CUTLASS pingpong for the pooler at m = 256; their notes say no custom path beat cuBLAS by more than about 1 us and a persistent stream-K kernel lost four judged checks |

Their proj memo lists, almost item for item, why ours costs 10 us more at small m: a
cross-CTA split-K reduction in the compressed path, escapes on the critical path, a capped
escape table, and global partials with a ticket. Those are exactly the mechanisms our ruled-out
register records as losers; we concluded "split-K reductions above 8 tokens" and "software
compression" were dead ends, they concluded the reductions and the escape handling were the
problem and removed them.

### 3.4 Layer glue and launches

| | ours | theirs |
|---|---|---|
| launches at T <= 32 | 17-23 (14-16 main, 3-7 side) | 9, single stream |
| PDL | the four W4 kernels only; none of our proj, attention, router or boundary kernels triggers or is launched as a secondary, so SGLang's own PDL kernels gain nothing after ours | every launch: Triton glue with `launch_pdl`, sk2 with the first weight stages issued before `griddepcontrol.wait`, attention and MoE with the attribute; measured as a launch-latency win at T <= 32 and a 1% loss at T = 256, so off above 32 |
| glue kernels | SGLang's two boundary modules (4.7 + 3.5 us), torch `F.rms_norm` for the pre-expert norm (6.3 us on a [1, 4096] tensor), SGLang's routing kernel, our route_align, F.pad (two launches) | three Triton kernels, one program per token with 16 warps: boundary 1, route (sigmoid, bias, top-8, local ids, pre-expert norm), boundary 2; about 4.4 us each |
| overlap | router, routing and route_align on a side stream under the pooler (our X1) | none; PDL overlaps tails and heads on one stream |
| unpooler at T <= 8 | the 1024-row slice, then F.pad (fixed by X5, held back on a rounding question that today's read of SGLang's kernel settles) | the slice; the boundary reads the 1024 live columns |
| what lost for them, judged | | fusing glue into a last-CTA tail of the GEMVs (o launch 9 to 49 us: one CTA's serial instruction stream), a boundary prologue that recomputes the norm in every CTA (+13 us at T = 1), a grid barrier at the end of a PDL-chained kernel (3-5 us), PDL above T = 32, routing fused into the pooler kernel |

### 3.5 Method

- Candidate chains timed in the layer at prepare time: per token count, the tuner captures
  and replays each dense backend, the MoE kernel against Marlin, and the glue variants with a
  cold-L2 sweep, then pins picks (`PIN_PICK`) where the isolated timing disagreed with the
  chain. Ours tunes the W4 configs the same way, and routes everything else by tables taken
  from the component problems' checks.
- A composition tool embeds the standalone attention and MoE files into the layer
  byte-identically, so a component win lands in the layer without a port. Ours carries hand
  copies made by `tools/dl_attn_inline.py` and `tools/dl_ws_inline.py`.
- Every new path is self-tested in prepare and gated off unless it wins on the chain, so a
  losing idea costs one check and never ships. Ours is the same in spirit (`_try`, self-tests),
  without the chain timing.
- Iteration depth: their attention source is tagged v298, the MoE v216, the proj v141; the
  memos record switch-level measurements ("ST1F 3 measured best: b16 full 93 to 91.5 us vs
  6"). Our two days produced 75 checks across four problems. They also started earlier: the
  memos are dated from Oct 25 and the repo was created Oct 27; the version numbers point at
  work from the opening day.

## 4. What we could have done, in the order it would have paid

1. Day one, attention: the fixed-frame atomic merge with a key-count ticket. It removes the
   combine launch on every verify shape and the cluster merge on sliding ones, and it is the
   precondition for one-tile-per-CTA plans at batch 1. Our stamps already showed the merge at
   5.9k cycles for 1k cycles of arithmetic; we read that as a DSMEM cost and pushed partials
   instead of asking whether a merge was needed.
2. Day one, layer: PDL on every kernel we own, with weight prologues before the wait, and our
   own three glue kernels. Today's layer audit puts this at +0.03 for PDL and +0.033 for the
   norm alone; the public entry's 9-launch chain is the existence proof.
3. Day two, dense: the swap-AB orientation with no cross-CTA reduction (`sk2`) for m = 8-32,
   and 12-bit weights with escape warps. We built the compression and the mma kernel; the
   missing pieces were the orientation (weights as B so R can be 8-64 rows per CTA with 96-256
   CTAs streaming full K) and moving escapes off the compute warps.
4. Days two to four, MoE: the single persistent launch with redundant routing and bulk-copied
   units, then register-A wgmma above 16 tokens. The MoE audit's hot-expert design reaches the
   same place by a different route (dequant once into smem, multicast token slabs); theirs is
   simpler because A stays in registers and N is capped at 64.
5. Throughout: a chain tuner in prepare, so one check compares many variants in the layer
   where PDL overlap and the judge's routing decide the winner.
6. Sliding shapes: treat code size and cold loads as the cost. Hoist every cold load into
   one group, one `sincosf` body, no dead paths in the once-per-launch code.

## 5. What they did that we missed entirely

- The fixed-frame merge and the QK-norm bound that makes it exact. We discussed fixed shifts
  (backlog, A1) and never connected the bound to deleting the merge.
- Speculating the sequence length from `page_table.shape[1]` at batch 1, a shape and therefore
  legal, verified on the device after the index group lands; it removes one dependent cold
  round trip from the batch-1 chain.
- The flat full-context kernel: equal key shares across all requests with a boundary penalty,
  so the 264 CTAs finish together regardless of per-request lengths. We split per request and
  per power-of-two split count.
- FP8 P.V on wgmma with eight ones-rows in V^T producing the row sums, and keys permuted into
  P's register order so P needs no shuffle; V transposed by `ldmatrix.trans`, `prmt`,
  `stmatrix`. We converted V to f16 in the loader warps (800 cycles per tile) and ruled FP8
  P.V out on mma.sync evidence.
- Register-A wgmma for the MoE, which is what makes 64-token jobs cheap; our large-tile test
  used mma.sync and ran into the shared-memory port.
- One persistent MoE launch with a software grid barrier, per-job readiness flags, and
  counters that reset themselves by parity and generation; the first weight units issued
  before routing.
- Bulk-copied 36 KB weight units consumed through registers, with the first-of-ring issue by
  one thread and a helper warp for epilogues. Our TMA variant fed mma.sync through smem and
  paid a barrier round trip per stage.
- Escape warps for lossless compression, and row permutation to balance escapes.
- The weights-as-B swap in the skinny GEMM so no cross-CTA reduction is needed at m <= 32.
- A fused pooler + router launch at T <= 16, and one concatenated cuBLAS GEMM for pooler +
  router hi + router lo above 32 tokens.
- Cold-code engineering as a first-class concern on the latency-bound shapes.
- A chain tuner with pinned picks, and a composition tool.

## 6. What we did that they did not, and what both of us found

- Both found the same losers: last-CTA glue tails (their o launch 9 to 49 us; our cluster
  finalizer and scratch-buffer split-K), warp-specialized producer rings for the MoE at small
  T (their note "small builds lose 1-2%" with RLOAD; our TMA kernel), PDL above T = 32 as a
  loss, and cluster launches that fail on GPC packing at size 8-16 (their clusters are unused
  for scored shapes; our 16-CTA cluster is non-portable and costs a cluster barrier).
- Our FP32-accumulator attention path keeps the error below FA3's (3.8e-5 to 6.4e-5 against
  FP64 on the same queries); their q_len 8 path rounds P to E4M3 as FA3's FP8 path does. Both
  are inside the rules; ours is the more conservative reading and costs about 8% on full
  verify. Their q_len 1 path pre-scales queries into f16 without E4M3 rounding, which is finer
  than ours.
- Our W4 numerics are closer to FP32 than Marlin's (4.2e-3 vs 5.3e-3) with BF16 rounding at
  SGLang's three points; theirs match the same points (gate/up, inter, y).
- Our route-on-side (X1) and X5 boundary are real wins that they got by other means (one
  stream with PDL; a boundary that reads 1024 columns).
- Our evidence discipline (every losing experiment with a job id and what it rules out) is
  the same discipline their notes show; the difference is which hypotheses were on the list.

## 7. Would our path have reached 2.1x by Nov 4

The honest projection from today's four audits, each on the existing kernels:

| step | score | time |
|---|---|---|
| today | 1.403 | |
| layer orchestration (own norm kernel, X5 with SGLang's rounding, PDL across our chain, L2 prefetch, own boundaries, router at T >= 16) | 1.50-1.52 | 2 days |
| MoE small items (SwiGLU in GEMM1's epilogue, dense block indexing, T = 1 configs) | 1.53-1.55 | 1-2 days |
| attention diet on sliding (code size, hoisted loads, new token under tile 0, in-kernel q_len 8 merge) | 1.58-1.62 | 3-4 days |

That is the ceiling of the path we were on, and it lands below rank 100 on today's board
(2.07x) and well below rank 50 on the board as it will stand on Nov 4 (2.14x today, rising
about 0.1x per day over the last three days). The rest of the distance is the three structural
rewrites: a one-launch attention family (their 2.61x against our 1.32x on that board), a
persistent register-A-wgmma MoE (2.33x against 1.70x), and the no-reduction skinny GEMM with
escape warps (1.50x against 1.14x). Each is three to six days of expert work by the audits'
estimates; the public entry's version counters say the same. Two days of our schedule went
into the FP32 attention precision question, A1, DS3, TMA weights and large tiles, all of which
were measurements inside the old structures and all of which came back inside the interval.

The decision that cost the most was not any single experiment; it was porting SGLang's
arrangement and optimizing each kernel in place, when the per-shape budget says the
arrangement itself (launch count, merges, reductions, side streams) is a third of the time at
decode 1 and the kernels' structures are the rest.

# Porting the fused MoE kernel into muse_decode_layer

The routed-experts block of `muse_moe_w4a16/submission.py` is one CUDA launch per call. This
guide gives what a layer needs to drop it in: the tensors, the scratch, the prepare steps, the
launch, and the points where it rounds to bf16. The kernel source is `_CUDA_SRC` in that
file; the host entry is `moe_run`.

## What one launch does

Grid = SM count (132 on H200), one CTA per SM, no cooperative launch (the shared-memory
footprint guarantees co-residency). Each CTA:

1. Routing prologue, run redundantly by every CTA from `topk_ids`: local expert id per entry
   (`id - local_start` when in `[0, local_count)`, else -1), a histogram, pair-row offsets
   (expert-major; entry i gets pair row `pos[i]`), and a job list.
2. Phase A: GEMM1 over the job's tokens for the job's expert, SwiGLU applied in the epilogue.
3. Phase B: GEMM2 over the SwiGLU output, writing FP32 `y * (1 + post_norm_w)` to `ybuf` and
   accumulating each pair row's sum of squares into `ss`.
4. A software grid barrier (atomic counter, generation-indexed).
5. The final pass: `out[t] = sum over local slots s of topk_w[t, s] * rsqrt(ss[q] / 4096 + eps)
   * ybuf[q]` with `q = pos[8 t + s]`, rounded to bf16. Tokens with no local slot get zeros.

Two kernels share this structure and the routing code:

- `moe_fused_kernel<SPLIT>` (288 threads: 8 compute warps and a helper warp) for M <= 16.
  Jobs are up to 8 tokens of one expert (an expert with more tokens becomes several jobs that
  re-stream its weights). A unit is 16 weight rows over the full K, one 36,864-byte bulk copy
  into a 4-slot ring; the 8 warps split K and use `mma.sync m16n8k16` with the job's x rows in
  registers; the helper warp sums the warps' partials and runs the epilogue.
- `moe_main_kernel` (576 threads: 4 consumer warpgroups, a weights producer thread and an x
  producer thread) for M >= 17. Jobs are up to 64 tokens; a unit is 256 rows streamed in 16
  stages of 256 k; consumers run register-A `wgmma m64nNk16` (N = 8 x ceil(tokens / 8)) with
  the stage's x in shared memory; stages are split over CTAs by a cost table (stream-K) and
  units cut between CTAs are summed through a global fixup slot. The weights ring has 5, 4 or
  3 slots of 36 KB next to 3 x slots of 8, 16 or 32 KB, chosen per launch from the largest
  job's N (every CTA derives the same sizes in its routing prologue).

The skinny kernel is built in several variants (`SKINNY_VARIANTS`: 8 or 16 compute warps, 4
or 5 ring slots, and loads-only diagnostic modes that stream the weights without computing);
the fat kernel in a computing and a loads-only mode. `prepare` times every computing variant
per batch size (graph replay, cold L2, synthetic routings) and keeps the fastest as
`state["policy"]`, keyed by the sizes in `POLICY_BS`; `kernel_fn` looks the variant up by M.
Without a policy entry, M >= `MAIN_MIN_M` (17) runs the fat kernel when `state["main_ok"]`
holds (the self-test clears it if the fat path fails), else the split skinny path, which
handles every size. The previous kernel (per-warp register-path mma.sync GEMMs, check
a49578e5c30348bb) is kept as `_run_legacy` with its tuned configs for 32, 128 and 256 tokens
(`LEGACY_POLICIES`, variant ids from `VARIANT_LEGACY0`); it is a bench candidate from 16
tokens up and needs its own weight layout (`_legacy_prepare`, 906 MB) and two more
extensions. Once the fused kernel wins everywhere it can be dropped.

## Tensors the layer must pass

Inputs per call (all on the same device, contiguous):

| name | dtype, shape | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `x` | bf16 [M, 4096] | the MoE block's input rows |
| `topk_ids` | int32 [M, 8] | global expert ids; 16-byte aligned (torch allocations are) |
| `topk_w` | float32 [M, 8] | routing weights as given |
| `out` | bf16 [M, 4096] | written in full |

Weights and constants prepared once (`prepare`), per local expert range `[lo, lo + nloc)`,
`nloc <= 32`:

| name | dtype, shape | made by |
|---|---|---|
| `w13` | uint8 [nloc, 512, 36864] | `repack_expert(packed, sf, 1)` per expert: 16-row units, 8 gate rows then their 8 up rows |
| `w2` | uint8 [nloc, 256, 36864] | `repack_expert(packed, sf, 2)` |
| `w13f` | uint8 [nloc, 32, 16, 36864] | `repack_expert_fat(packed, sf, 1)`: 256-row units x 16 stages |
| `w2f` | uint8 [nloc, 16, 16, 36864] | `repack_expert_fat(packed, sf, 2)` |
| `gs13`, `gs2` | float32 [nloc] | the global scales, as given |
| `nw` | float32 [4096] | `1 + post_norm_w` in FP32 |

The repacks permute bits and bytes only; the values stay NVFP4 (E2M1 codes and E4M3 block
scales). `scales_ok` must hold (positive normal E4M3 scales), which the challenge's weights
satisfy; otherwise the dequant's PRMT + IMAD scale trick is inexact and the kernel must not be
used. The two repacks hold 906 MB each for 32 experts.

Scratch allocated once (`_scratch`), reused by every launch; nothing is reset between
launches from the host:

| name | dtype, shape | role |
|---|---|---|
| `inter` | bf16 [4096, 4096] | SwiGLU output by pair row (skinny path) |
| `ybuf` | float32 [4096, 4096] | GEMM2 output times (1 + w), by pair row |
| `ss` | float32 [2, 4096] | sums of squares, double-buffered by the launch generation |
| `ctr` | int32 [64] | ctr[3] generation, ctr[4], ctr[5] the two barrier counters, ctr[8] spin-timeout flags |
| `done_a` | int32 [544] | per job, phase A units finished (skinny path) |
| `xa`, `xb` | uint8 [(512 + 96) x 65536] | fat path: x rows and SwiGLU output in the per-stage wgmma B layout |
| `fix` | float32 [2 x SMs x 4 x 128 x 32] | fat path: fixup slots for units cut between CTAs |
| `fixcnt` | int32 [2 x SMs x 4] | their stage counts |
| `xready` | int32 [96] | fat path: gathered x rows per job |
| `done_as` | int32 [96 x 16] | fat path: finished phase A units per (job, phase B stage) |

Sizes assume at most 512 tokens per launch (`CHUNK_TOKENS`); `moe_run` splits larger M into
launches of 512. Every per-launch flag is reset inside the launch (after the grid barrier, or
by the finisher that used it), and the barrier counter and `ss` copy alternate with the
generation, so graph replays need no host-side memset.

## Prepare steps

1. `_repack(weights, lo, nloc)`: both layouts and the global scales, about 1 s on GPU.
2. `nw = (post_norm_w.float() + 1)`.
3. `_scratch(device)`.
4. Build the extension once (`_ext()`, one `load_inline`, about 40 s; the fat path's wgmma
   wrappers are generated by `_wgmma_code()`).
5. Self-test against the FP32 reference: every computing skinny variant at M = 1, 4, 8, 16
   and the fat path at 32, 33, 128, 257, normal and skewed routings; the tolerance is 8e-3
   relative L2 (measured 3.8e-3 to 4.6e-3; the judge allows 1.5e-2). A spin timeout in any
   launch (ctr[8] != 0) fails the test. A failing fat path sets `main_ok = False`.
6. The variant bench (`_bench`) and the policy, then the policy's variants once more at every
   test size.

The judge gives `prepare` 300 s; the whole of the above takes about 60 to 90 s (the build is
the largest part).

## The launch

`moe_run(x, topk_ids, topk_w, w13, w2, gs13, gs2, nw, inter, ybuf, ss, ctr, done_a, out,
w13f, w2f, xa, xb, fix, fixcnt, xready, done_as, lo, nloc, eps, variant, cost)` with `variant`
an index into `SKINNY_VARIANTS` (skinny, split jobs of 8 tokens) or `VARIANT_MAIN0 + i` with
`MAIN_MODES[i]` the fat mode, and `cost` either `[]` (the compiled stream-K stage costs) or 18
ints, `cost[9 * phase + ntt]` for ntt 1 to 8 (entries 0 and 9 unused). Since 2026-10-28 (commit
068b3ce) the cost argument is required; a layer port made from an earlier file passes `[]`.
Fat modes: 0 wgmma for every job; 6 jobs of up to 2 n8 tiles on mma.sync, the rest on wgmma;
12, 13, 14 are 6, 0 and 6 with fence.acq_rel.gpu in place of fence.sc.gpu in the epilogue and
fixup, 14 also with two mma.sync accumulator chains; 1 streams only; 11 is 6 with clock stamps
written to `inter` (never a policy choice). `VARIANT_FIT0 + i` in Python runs `VARIANT_MAIN0 +
i` with the costs fitted from the stamps in prepare (`state["fit_cost"]`).
`_vname(variant)` gives the name the bench prints. It launches on the current stream, is graph-capturable (no
host syncs, no allocation, no value-dependent branching on the host), and needs the whole GPU:
the grid barrier spins until all 132 CTAs arrive, so nothing else may occupy SMs for the
launch's duration, and a PDL successor that starts early would share SMs with the spinning
CTAs. In the layer, launch it alone on the main stream, with the router and the pre-expert
norm complete; the layer's own `topk_ids` and `topk_weights` tensors pass straight through.

A wait that lasts longer than 2^31 cycles (about a second) marks ctr[8] and gives up instead
of hanging; the result is then wrong. Read ctr[8] after a self-test, never inside the timed
path.

Both kernels begin with `griddepcontrol.wait`, so a launch with the programmatic dependent
launch attribute is safe (they do not touch their inputs before the previous kernel has
completed); without the attribute the instruction does nothing. They never call
`griddepcontrol.launch_dependents`, so a successor launched with the attribute starts only
when they finish.

| 1 | sk8w4s | 29.3 | 46.7 |
| 8 | sk8w4s | 68.4 | 87.5 |
| 16 | sk8w4s | 97.3 | 107.4 |

Every variant passes the FP32 self-test at M = 1 to 257 on normal and skewed routings, so the
kernel can be switched on at every T; at T = 128 the policy itself falls back to the previous
kernel, so the layer loses nothing there. In the layer, keep the bench in `prepare` (its
routing differs from the standalone problem's, and the choice between `legacy128`, `main-d2`
and `sk8w4s` at 32 to 256 tokens is within 10%), and trim the build: `MAIN_MODES = (0,)` and
`SKINNY_VARIANTS = ((8, 4, 0), (16, 4, 0))` cut the 140 s build to about half, which the
layer's own 300 s prepare budget needs.

## Where the numbers round to bf16

These follow SGLang's Marlin path, which the activation rule in TASK.md pins:

- GEMM1 accumulates in FP32 over the full K (inside one CTA on the skinny path, over the
  stream-K shares on the fat path). Gate and up are rounded to bf16 before SiLU
  (`bf16r(acc * gs13 * 128)`), SwiGLU's output is stored as bf16 (`inter` or `xb`).
- GEMM2 accumulates in FP32; its output is rounded to bf16 before the norm
  (`bf16r(acc * gs2 * 128)`), then multiplied by `(1 + w)` in FP32 and stored as FP32 in
  `ybuf`; the sum of squares uses those FP32 values.
- The final pass sums `topk_w * rsqrt(ss / 4096 + 1e-8) * y` in FP32 and rounds once to
  bf16.
- The dequant itself is exact: an E2M1 code times its E4M3 block scale is formed in bf16 with
  no rounding (at most 6 significant bits), and the global scale times 2^7 is applied in FP32
  in the epilogue.

## What the layer must not change

- Pair-row order is internal (expert-major, then entry order); outputs do not depend on it.
- Sums of squares are FP32 atomics, so bitwise results vary run to run at the last bit.
- The routing prologue assumes `topk_ids` holds global ids and filters to the local range;
  pass the ids the router emits, not local ids.
- The x tiles (xa, xb) cross from generic stores to other CTAs' `cp.async.bulk` reads. Each
  writer fences with `fence.proxy.async.global` before its release and each issuing thread
  again after its acquire; the gather publishes with `red.release` after its barrier. Keep
  all of it (docs/runs-moe.md, "Proxy ordering of the x tiles").
- The layer's copy is generated by `tools/dl_moe_inline.py`, which builds only the fat modes in
  its `LAYER_MODES` (mode 0 as of 2026-10-29). The layer's host wrapper zeroes `Params::cost`
  (the compiled stage-cost table); the struct is not zero-initialized, so a port must set it.

# Open Kernel Challenge — Paper-Derived Experiment Backlog

**Snapshot:** October 27, 2026, late night Pacific; some repository logs are dated October 28 UTC.  
**Repository:** https://github.com/yelgabo/okc  
**Purpose:** Research candidates for the existing H200 project, not a restart or authorization to submit.  
**Evidence labels:** MEASURED = user/repository measurements; DERIVED = calculations from inspected code; PUBLISHED = source method; HYPOTHESIS = proposed adaptation; GATE = suggested decision threshold, not a predicted gain.

## Executive decision

Keep the in-progress FP32-accumulator-mode/FP32-softmax attention check first. After that, choose the next attention experiment from its measured critical path:

- **Consumer/softmax limited:** A1 bounded-shift rescaling; then A5 inter-warpgroup staggering.
- **Loader/resource limited:** A2 shared-memory lifetime compaction; then A4 row-granular TMA only after an address-layout and instruction-cost audit.
- **Short sliding-window workloads:** A3 in-kernel split merge is a separate opportunity with a measured merge-cost target.

Retain the two already queued MoE experiments, but sharpen them: M1 hot/cold expert tile selection and M2 packed-weight TMA. Do not call them newly discovered ideas. Add B1 hardware-compressible BF16 allocation as a capability-gated architectural probe, not as a promised optimization.

**Important changes from the earlier reading list:** Stream-K is conditional on demonstrated work imbalance, not the default remedy for repeated hot-expert weight reads. FlashDecoding++ has a recomputation fallback; importing just its fixed softmax shift would omit an essential part. SonicMoE's token-rounding router changes real routing and is not an acceptable shortcut here.

No GPU experiments were run for this research. A small CPU-only numerical check of A1's algebra was run; its scope is recorded below.

## 1. Baseline to preserve

The user's latest submitted results are BF16 projections **1.139x**, MoE **1.699x**, attention **1.291x**, and integrated decode **1.390x**. The **1.348x attention result is checked, not submitted**, and uses FP16 Q.K accumulation and half2 softmax. The precision-conservative replacement is still in progress in this snapshot.

The W4A16 integrated-layer port and the score-weighting fix are complete. Do not create tasks to redo either. The whole-layer W4 path passed 13/13 tests, has no shape regressions, and uses approximately 95.5 seconds of the 300-second preparation allowance. Programmatic dependent launch makes individual kernel durations unsuitable for additive latency forecasts.

**Terminology caveat:** NVIDIA documents that FP8 `wgmma.mma_async` with `.f32` destination currently accumulates internally at precision above half but below single precision [R12].
